newsitem.title: ITALY: Global powers debate key grain reserve levels.
newsitem.headline: Global powers debate key grain reserve levels.

text.p: The top five global cereals exporters and developing nations that are their biggest customers began talks on Wednesday to try to agree how much grain the world should keep in reserve in case of food emergencies.

The meeting, at the Rome headquarters of the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), brings together senior officials from the United States, Canada, the European Union, Australia, Argentina and more than 50 other states to discuss grain policy.
"It will probably be a lively debate," Myles Mielke, secretary of the Intergovernmental Group on Grains, said before the meeting opened. The group gathers every two years.

Plunging grain stocks last year, which drove wheat and corn prices to record highs and stockpiles to 20-year lows, set alarm bells ringing and prompted calls for change to the mechanism set up to try to guarantee food security after crises in the 1970s.
Using the FAO's current warning system, the danger area is reached when grain stocks fall below 17 percent to 18 percent of a year's average consumption -- some eight weeks supply.

But grain stock levels have slumped rapidly from a high of some 21 percent of consumption in the course of three years in which production failed to meet consumption. Levels are only now begining to be replenished.
The FAO forecasts that supplies fell to 14.3 percent in 1995-96 and will still be only 15.8 percent in 1996-97 despite bumper harvests in Australia and the EU.

"That still depends on a good 1997 crop. Harvests look good and crop development looks good, it has all the makings of an increasing ratio next year but who knows what will happen," said Werner Lamade, Chief of FAO's Basic Foodstuffs Service.
He said in an interview that the warning system, which is based on highly sensitive political considerations, had been "a thorn in the flesh" of many countries.
Developing nations, which account for some three-quarters of grain imports, would like the world's silos to have sufficient stockpiles to provide buffer against all shortfalls.
Exporters, however, are prepared to gamble that serious shorfalls occur rarely enough to allow them to live with lower levels of reserves.
"It depends on what level of risk governments are willing to take and there's no consensus on what risk level is acceptable," Mielke said.
The FAO, which has conducted a number of different analyses, will argue that there is no pressing need to change the system.
"We would be quite happy if (the meeting) could agree on 17-18 percent. We think this is still a reasonable figure," Lamade said. He said commodities markets seemed to agree.
"Some have noted that whenever there is a fall below (the 17-18 percent threshold, prices go up. When (stocks) go above, prices settle," he said.

The meeting, which runs until Friday, will also evaluate the recent rollercoaster ride in cereals prices and the extent to which price instability may increase in future as countries change their cereals policy to meet Uruguay Round conditions.

The 1986-93 Uruguay Round of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) set global rules for agricultural produce for the first time and gradually reduces subsidy spending and volumes by major exporters for six years from 1995-96.
